why: OVERCLAIM a hostile reader dismantles with a concordance
old: The ordinary first-century word for a Christian was not believer, and it was certainly not convert. It was the elect — hoi eklektoi, the chosen ones.
new: Among the ordinary names the first Christians answered to — alongside brothers, saints, disciples — was one nobody reaches for now. They were the elect: hoi eklektoi, the chosen ones. It is worth noticing which of those four fell out of use, and roughly when.

why: CENTRAL FACTUAL CLAIM FALSE. Copernicus kept the epicycles; he removed the equant.
old: When Copernicus moved the center from Earth to the Sun, something remarkable happened: the epicycles disappeared. The planets' motions became simple, elegant, describable by basic laws. The retrograde motion that seemed inexplicable suddenly made perfect sense. It wasn't the planets moving backwards. It was the perspective. When you move the center, the universe becomes clear.
new: And here is the part of the story almost everyone gets wrong, which is also the part that matters. Copernicus did not make astronomy simpler. He kept the circles. His system needed roughly as many of them as Ptolemy's, and for decades it predicted no better. What he removed was one ugly device called the equant, and what he offered in its place was not accuracy but sense: the retrograde loop stopped being something the planets did and became something the observer was doing. It was not the planets moving backwards. It was the perspective. The ellipses that finally made the mathematics beautiful were Kepler's, and they were sixty-six years away.

why: Invalid inference resting on the false premise
old: And the elegance of it is itself evidence. In science, when one model requires epicycles and another doesn't, the simpler model is usually true. Heliocentric astronomy was simpler. So is the theology of sovereign grace.
new: Which makes it the more interesting witness, not the weaker one. Heliocentrism did not win because it was tidier. It won because it was true, and it had to outlast two generations of men who could point at the arithmetic and say, correctly, that it had bought them nothing yet. A thing can be right and inconvenient and unrewarding for sixty years. Worth remembering the next time the comfort of a doctrine is offered as an argument for it.

why: Jupiter's moons did not establish heliocentrism
old: Galileo saw Jupiter's moons through a telescope and knew the model was wrong.
new: Galileo turned a telescope on Jupiter in 1610 and found four bodies going round something that was not the Earth — which did not prove the Earth moved, but did prove that not everything circled the man doing the looking.
